hints: Think about what must stay the same on both sides of a nuclear equation, and recall what an alpha-particle is made from in terms of protons and neutrons.
Add the protons from Np-237 and the alpha-particle to get the protons of X, do the same for total nucleons, then use neutrons = nucleons - protons.
walkthrough:
**Remember what an alpha-particle carries away**
An alpha-particle is a helium-4 nucleus, $^{4}_{2}He$. That means it carries away $2$ protons and $4$ nucleons in total ($2$ protons + $2$ neutrons). In any decay, total proton number $Z$ and total nucleon number $A$ are conserved.

**Rebuild the parent nucleus X**
For protons: $$Z_X = Z_{Np} + Z_{\alpha} = 93 + 2 = 95$$ For nucleons: $$A_X = A_{Np} + A_{\alpha} = 237 + 4 = 241$$ So X has $95$ protons and mass number $241$.

**Get neutrons by subtraction**
Neutrons $N = A - Z$: $$N = 241 - 95 = 146$$
Final answer: number of protons = 95, number of neutrons = 146

hints: The parent was stationary, so total momentum was zero. Think about what that means for the momenta of the two products after the split.
walkthrough:
**Momentum must still balance**
You start with a stationary nucleus, so total momentum is zero. After decay the alpha-particle shoots off one way with momentum $p$. To keep total momentum zero, the heavy Np nucleus must recoil the opposite way with equal and opposite momentum.

**Moving means kinetic energy**
Because the recoiling Np nucleus is moving, it must carry some kinetic energy, $E_k = p^2 / 2m$. The total $5.5\text{ MeV}$ released is therefore shared between the alpha-particle and the Np nucleus. A small part may also be emitted as gamma radiation. So the alpha-particle alone gets less than $5.5\text{ MeV}$.
Final answer: Some of the 5.5 MeV is transferred to the Np nucleus as kinetic energy (recoil) to conserve momentum, and/or as gamma-ray photon energy.

hints: Start from the basic idea of current as total charge passing a point divided by time. Focus on finding the total charge carried by all the alpha-particles.
Remember each alpha-particle carries charge $+2e$ where $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$. Combine $N = 6.9 \times 10^{11}$, $t = 30\text{ s}$ and this charge.
walkthrough:
**Write current as charge per second**
Current is the rate of flow of charge: $$I = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{Nq}{t}$$ where $N$ is number of particles and $q$ is charge per particle.

**Put in the alpha charge and numbers**
Each alpha has $q = 2e = 2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$. $$I = \frac{(6.9 \times 10^{11}) \times (2 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19})}{30}$$ $$I = 7.36 \times 10^{-9}\text{ A} \approx 7.4 \times 10^{-9}\text{ A}$$

hints: Think of power as total energy released divided by time. First work out the total energy from the number of decays and the energy per decay.
Convert the $5.5\text{ MeV}$ per decay into joules using $1\text{ eV} = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J}$, then divide the total by $30\text{ s}$.
walkthrough:
**Total energy then divide by time**
Power is energy per unit time: $$P = \frac{\text{total energy}}{t} = \frac{N \times E_{1}}{t}$$ where $E_1 = 5.5\text{ MeV}$ is the energy per decay.

**Convert MeV to joules and calculate**
$$E_1 = 5.5 \times 10^{6} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ J} = 8.8 \times 10^{-13}\text{ J}$$ Then: $$P = \frac{(6.9 \times 10^{11}) \times (5.5 \times 10^{6} \times 1.60 \times 10^{-19})}{30}$$ $$P \approx 0.020\text{ W}$$
